summary.text: Superconductivity is a set of properties of materials in which electrical resistance is exactly zero and magnetic fields are expelled.
Below a critical temperature the resistance drops abruptly to zero, so a current in a loop of superconducting wire can persist indefinitely with no power source.
It can only be explained by quantum mechanics, and the Meissner effect shows it is more than the classical idea of a perfect conductor.

facts.label: Discovered
facts.value: 1911, by Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes

facts.label: First material
facts.value: Mercury, whose resistance vanished at 4.2 K

facts.label: YBCO ceramic
facts.value: Critical temperature of 92 K, above liquid nitrogen's boiling point

facts.label: Cuprate surprise
facts.value: In 1986, ceramics were found superconducting above 35 K

facts.label: Liquid nitrogen
facts.value: A cheap coolant that boils at 77 K

items.prompt: As a copper wire is cooled, its resistance falls gradually. What is different for a superconductor?

options.label: Its resistance rises at first, then levels off
Its resistance falls slowly but never reaches zero
Its resistance stays the same at any temperature
Its resistance drops abruptly to zero below a critical temperature

items.explain: Unlike an ordinary conductor, a superconductor has a critical temperature below which resistance drops abruptly to zero.

items.prompt: A ring of superconducting wire is given a current and then disconnected from the battery. What happens to the current?

options.label: It can persist indefinitely with no power source
It fades within seconds like an ordinary wire
It reverses direction every cycle
It spreads out into the surrounding air

items.explain: A current through a loop of superconducting wire can persist indefinitely with no power source.

items.prompt: A superconductor is cooled below its critical temperature while sitting in a magnetic field. What happens to the field inside the material?

options.label: It doubles in strength
It is completely cancelled in the interior
It spins around the edge only
It stays exactly as it was

items.explain: The Meissner effect is the complete cancellation of the magnetic field in the interior as the material enters the superconducting state.

items.prompt: Why can't superconductivity be dismissed as just a wire with perfect conduction in the classical sense?

options.label: Classical wires always have some resistance, however cold
The Meissner effect shows it is not merely idealized classical perfect conductivity
Superconductors only work in space
Perfect conductors cannot carry current at all

items.explain: The Meissner effect indicates superconductivity cannot be understood simply as the idealization of perfect conductivity in classical physics.

items.prompt: Why was a material that superconducts at 92 K a big practical gain for labs?

options.label: It needs no cooling at all
It works only with rare and costly liquid helium
It could be cooled with cheap liquid nitrogen
It makes magnets weaker and lighter

items.explain: Liquid nitrogen boils at 77 K, so a critical temperature of 92 K meant this cheap coolant could be used as a refrigerant.

items.prompt: Why are the 1986 ceramics called high-temperature superconductors?

options.label: They work at ordinary room temperature
They were heated in a furnace while forming
They were found near hot volcanic rock
Their transition temperature is impossible for conventional ones

items.explain: Such a high transition temperature is theoretically impossible for a conventional superconductor, so the materials were termed high-temperature.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Superconductivity is a set of properties seen in materials called superconductors, whose electrical resistance is exactly zero and which push magnetic fields out of themselves. An ordinary metal's resistance falls bit by bit as it gets colder, even close to absolute zero. A superconductor behaves differently. It has a critical temperature, and below that point its resistance suddenly drops to nothing. So a current sent round a loop of superconducting wire can keep flowing indefinitely with no power source.

paragraphs.heading: A sudden drop in mercury
paragraphs.text: The Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found the effect in solid mercury on April 8, 1911. He was studying how mercury resists current at very low temperatures, using newly produced liquid helium to cool it. At 4.2 K he saw the resistance vanish all at once. Other materials followed: tin and lead in 1913, at 3.8 K and 7 K, and niobium nitride at 16 K in 1941.

paragraphs.heading: Pushing magnetic fields out
paragraphs.text: In 1933 Meissner and Ochsenfeld found that superconductors drive out magnetic fields applied to them, which became known as the Meissner effect. As a material turns superconducting, the magnetic field inside it is cancelled completely. This shows superconductivity is more than the classical ideal of a perfect conductor. Like ferromagnetism and the spectral lines of atoms, it can only be explained by quantum mechanics.

paragraphs.heading: Explaining how it works
paragraphs.text: In the 1950s theorists came to understand conventional superconductivity through two theories: Ginzburg–Landau theory in 1950 and BCS theory in 1957. Also in 1950, researchers found that a superconductor's critical temperature depends on the isotopic mass of its element. That clue suggested the electron–phonon interaction was the underlying microscopic cause. BCS theory, from Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer, pictured the current as a superfluid of Cooper pairs, which are pairs of electrons that interact by exchanging phonons. The three received the Nobel Prize in 1972.

paragraphs.heading: Warmer superconductors
paragraphs.text: In 1986 some cuprate-perovskite ceramics were found to have critical temperatures above 35 K (−238 °C). Soon after, Ching-Wu Chu swapped the lanthanum for yttrium to make YBCO, lifting the critical temperature to 92 K (−181 °C). Such a high value is impossible in theory for a conventional superconductor, so these became known as high-temperature superconductors. The jump mattered because liquid nitrogen, a cheap coolant that boils at 77 K (−196 °C), could now do the cooling, which makes many experiments and uses more practical.

paragraphs.heading: Switches and magnets
paragraphs.text: The first practical use came in 1954, when Dudley Allen Buck invented the cryotron. It pairs two superconductors with very different critical magnetic fields to make a quick, simple switch for computer parts. Kamerlingh Onnes tried to build an electromagnet with superconducting windings soon after his discovery, but fairly weak magnetic fields wrecked the superconductivity of his materials. Yntema managed a small 0.7-tesla iron-core electromagnet wound with superconducting niobium wire. Wernick found that niobium–tin at 4.2 kelvin could carry over 100,000 amperes per square centimeter in a field of 8.8 tesla.
